The post Z AI Releases GLM-5.4: A 750B Loop Transformer That Runs 28 Layers Twice appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Z.ai has released GLM-5.4 , its first flagship model built on a Loop Transformer architecture. The GLM-5.4 Loop Transformer runs 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for 2 iterations. Z.ai says the model reaches intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models. For developers, the pitch is ‘Generalized Coding’: code as the tool for video, games, 3D shaders and CAD. TL;DR Size: 750B-scale base. Active parameters not disclosed. Context window not officially listed (the blog discusses deployment at 1M context). Runs on: Z.ai-hosted only for now (GLM Coding Plan, ZCode, Z.ai Chat). Self-hosting hardware not disclosed until weights ship. Performance: No flagship benchmark table yet. Z.ai claims parity with 2T-3T parameter models. Best: +11.3 points on AIME25 (19.17 to 30.42) in Z.ai’s 30B looped ablation. Worst: +3.3 points on IFBench (50.20 to 53.47), the smallest gain. Z.ai also flags “marathon thinking” loops. What is GLM-5.4? GLM-5.4 is a 750B-scale Loop Transformer from Z.ai that runs shared layers twice per pass. It ships first inside Z.ai’s own products: the GLM Coding Plan , the ZCode desktop app and Z.ai Chat . Z.ai did not pre-train a looped model from scratch. It adapted the pre-trained GLM-5 base through continued training. The technical post states that looped models trained from scratch still trail unshared models at equal compute. Adapting an existing base raises the ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead. How does the Loop Transformer work? In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In GLM-5.4, a group of 28 weight-shared layers runs for 2 iterations. Z.ai made 3 changes to keep this practical at 750B scale. Gated progressive updates Overwriting hidden states across loops made activation norms blow up. GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration. The first pass writes small updates and builds global context. The second pass opens the gates to refine the output. On harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively. Hybrid KV cache A naive design keeps a full KV cache for every loop. GLM-5.4’s second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in pass 1. It keeps its own new KV only inside a local sliding window. So the extra loop costs 1 sliding window of KV cache, not a full context cache. Z.ai says this keeps the cost increase over GLM-5.3 under control at 1M context. Sparse attention index reuse The second loop reuses the indices from the first loop’s indexer. That adds zero indexing overhead. Z.ai reports near-identical results versus recomputing indices on every pass. How does GLM-5.4 perform on benchmarks? Z.ai has not published benchmark scores for the 750B GLM-5.4 model. A Z.ai team member said scores will come later, per DataCamp . The evidence in the blog is an iso-parameter ablation on a 30B model. It shares the 750B base’s architecture. The looped version used about 10% more total training compute. Scores were measured after 200K long-context SFT with thinking mode on. Self-reported, 30B model, not the 750B flagship. Two patterns stand out. The largest gains come in math, science reasoning and long context. Output length also falls on most tasks. MMLU-Pro answers got 14.9% shorter and GPQA-Diamond answers 11.7% shorter. Z.ai says part of the reasoning moves into the loop’s implicit depth. AIME25 is the exception: output length dropped only 2%. Z.ai validated the design on 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B bases. The ‘2T-3T parameter’ claim has no flagship table behind it yet. What can GLM-5.4 do beyond traditional coding? Z.ai calls this direction Generalized Coding. It credits gains in both coding and vision. The post Meet Facebook’s Your Algorithm: How Meta Turns Plain-Language Preferences Into Ranking appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has published an engineering deep dive on Facebook Your Algorithm . Your Algorithm lets people tell Facebook, in plain language, what they want in Feed and Reels. Meta announced the feature on October 13, 2026. The new post shows how large language models (LLMs) sit inside a production recommender. For developers, it is a rare look at explicit preferences wired into an implicit-signal ranking stack. TL;DR What: ‘ Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations’ Runs on: Meta’s server-side ranking stack, plus on-device cache invalidation in the Facebook app. Best: Explicit interests feed 4 retrieval sources and apply across both Feed and Reels. Bottom line: Best: a clear blueprint for LLM-steered ranking What is Facebook Your Algorithm? Your Algorithm is an AI-powered preference page for Facebook Feed and Reels. It has 3 parts, per Meta’s engineering post . A one-sentence “Lately Summary” describes recent viewing. An “Interested In” list is prefilled from past activity. A “Not Interested In” list holds exclusions. Users can type interests, move them between lists, or delete them. Access is through the three-dot menu on posts, according to Meta’s newsroom . Meta’s framing is simple. Implicit engagement signals scale well but adapt slowly and miss nuance. Explicit, stated preferences close that gap. How does the Your Algorithm system work? Meta splits the preference lifecycle into 4 components: Profile generation: An LLM turns regularly refreshed interest signals into readable topic names. It also writes the Lately Summary. Preference management: An LLM checks that a typed phrase is a coherent topic. It detects duplicates and maps the phrase to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller, cheaper model. Ranking: Both lists are applied across the ranking funnel. Delivery optimization: Changes reach the feed faster. Validated interests are enriched with an embedding and search keywords. They are saved to a shared store that both Feed and Reels read. A separate component runs integrity and safety checks. How do “Interested In” topics reach the feed? Each interest drives 4 retrieval sources. 2 match content directly: search and clusters of closely related topics. 2 extend reach: the content graph and item-to-item similarity. A relevance check compares the interest’s meaning with each candidate. Passing candidates get a late-stage ranking promotion. A reranking control layer then stops flooding: Repeats of the same interest are spaced out. Each interest’s daily contribution is capped. Retrieval fetches for 1 interest per request. New interests get temporary extra weight. How does “Not Interested In” filtering work? Meta calls this layered filtering at every stage. Ranking uses embedding comparison to remove close matches. Demotion rules push down near matches. A fine-tuned LLM reranker then reviews the final list. Quality requests, such as less AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, take a different path. They map to dedicated demotion signals, not topic matching. Requests naming a creator filter that creator directly. On the client, cache invalidation removes queued items that match a new exclusion before display. Why use a small fine-tuned LLM as the reranker? The reranker is trained to return only the items to remove. Meta says this small fine-tuned model beat a general-purpose model judging each item. It was faster and more reliable. Outputting a short removal list is cheaper than scoring every candidate. Speed comes from a “supplementary tail load.” Adding an interest fires an extra fetch outside the normal cycle. Meta gives no latency figure for it. But perhaps equally crucial is the reverse consideration: What makes for a truly awful startup name? It’s a somewhat subjective exercise. Nonetheless, branding experts and occasional writers on the subject can agree on a few basic parameters. These include hard-sounding names, brands with negative connotations, and a certain ubiquitous suffix that could soon sound irrelevant. Below, we look at each of these categories in more detail No. 1: Harsh-sounding names One branding principle is that startups should avoid names that are unpleasant to pronounce. This includes words that sound too harsh or guttural, or are awkward in the native languages of potential users. Unfortunately, it’s a principle often ignored. For Athol Foden of naming consultancy Brighter Naming , the most prominent unpleasant brand name of recent quarters is Grok , the chatbot of Elon Musk ’s SpaceXSI . Foden hates it so much he devoted an entire essay to what’s wrong with it. “I still want to throw up when you say that name… and it is even worse in foreign languages,” he said in an interview. In his essay he called the brand a cross between “a suppressed swear word and a throat condition your doctor would prescribe antibiotics for.” It’s not an anti-Musk stance. Foden is a fan of the entrepreneur’s Starlink as a name choice for the global satellite Internet service. It’s memorable and evocative in a positive way. For other examples, we didn’t want to pick on current startups for their naming choices. So we looked instead to archives of startups past for other cases of harsh naming choices that didn’t pan out or are no longer operating under that brand. Our shortlist included Quibi , a heavily funded short video startup with famous founders and a famously short shelf life. Others that have either folded or no longer operate under the original brand include Doostang , Gtrot , and Xobni (inbox spelled backwards, but not terribly clear how to pronounce.) No. 2: Negative connotations Another naming tactic to avoid is selecting a brand that evokes negative imagery or connotations. “We always say: This is something you should be proud to wear on a hoodie,” said Bruno Benedini , co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight . If not, then reconsider. Following this notion, one recently funded company name that rubbed both Benedini and your author the wrong way is Warhound , a startup focused on breeding dogs for roles in the military, law enforcement and emergency response that recently raised $200 million . Sure, it’s memorable. But it sets an awfully aggressive tone, especially for a pet-pampering culture in which other startups promote offerings like dog spas, canine couture, and custom meals. While there’s a role for well-treated service dogs, it’s preferably far from any battlefield. Or, as Benedini put it, “I’d be embarrassed to have Warhound on my hoodie.” For other examples of less-than-stellar naming picks, we looked through the archives of startups past. One dud was Flud , which combines awkward spelling and imagery of a natural disaster. Boo.com , a defunct fashion site that was the iconic flops of the dot-com era also comes to mind, evoking fright more than the desire to shop. Another popular but questionable pick is Fire (sometimes alternately spelled Fyre), the chosen name of at least a dozen entries in the Crunchbase dataset. No. 3: AI suffixes It may still be in vogue to give your company a one-word name followed by AI. But don’t try to get a branding consultant to sign off on it. Both Foden and Benedini advise against adding AI to the company name for multiple reasons. One is that it will likely sound dated going forward. Another criticism is that since virtually every startup incorporates AI to some extent, adopting a name with “AI” isn’t particularly meaningful. If one does insist on an AI name, the minimum next step is to make sure it still works with those two letters on the end. Lots of companies — including Amazon (formerly Amazon.com ) and Apple (initially Apple Computer) — have altered their names to keep up with the times and done just fine. Or just ignore the advice Despite all the advice on how to avoid an awful name, a part of me can’t help hoping more startups will just ignore it all. Then we could live in a world where startups sought funding with names like “Gruesome Grok AI” or “Festering Boil Labs.” That said, there’s a reason startup naming is a serious endeavor, and bad choices often have equally bad consequences.
